youtube.aciklama:
How is a hearing aid cleaned, and how do moisture and earwax damage it? In this lesson we cover daily care, changing the wax guard, a step-by-step check of common faults such as a dead aid, weak sound, crackling and whistling, and how to use a listening stethoscope.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; Taylor and Mueller, Fitting and Dispensing Hearing Aids; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Moisture, earwax, filters and common faults
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the daily care of a hearing aid: moisture, earwax and changing the filter.
Then we will cover common faults such as a dead aid, weak sound and crackling, and the check done with a listening stethoscope.
Most hearing aid faults come not from an electronic failure but from simple problems of everyday use.
In this example we see a receiver-in-canal, or RIC, hearing aid.
The microphone inlets are on the top of the case; dust, hair spray and dirt can block these small openings over time.
Because the receiver sits inside the ear canal, it is the part most exposed to earwax and moisture.
The battery, or rechargeable cell, powers the whole system; a weak battery is the hidden cause of many faults.
The dome or earmold that goes into the ear is also a surface that carries wax and moisture directly.
So care is taught as a simple habit that takes a few minutes every day.

maddeler.metin: Clean the microphone inlet with a _brush_
Remove wax from dome and earmold

cumleler: After the aid is taken out each day, it is wiped with a dry, soft cloth.
The microphone inlets are gently cleaned with the small brush supplied with the aid, with the inlets facing down.
Earwax on the dome or earmold is removed with the brush or a cleaning wire.
A detachable earmold can be washed in lukewarm water as the manufacturer advises and refitted only when fully dry.
The aid itself is never put in water; alcohol or other cleaning products are not used unless the manufacturer recommends them.
At night the aid is kept in its case, in a dry place away from heat sources and out of children's reach.

yan.metin: The most common *hidden* cause of faults

cumleler: Moisture is the most common factor that damages the electronic circuit, microphone and receiver of a hearing aid.
Sweat, rain, bathroom steam and the condensation that forms when moving from a warm to a cold place all bring moisture to the aid.
In behind-the-ear aids, moisture can be seen as small water droplets inside the tubing to the earmold, and it can block the sound.
A drying box or desiccant capsule can be used at night to reduce moisture in the aid.
In battery aids, leaving the battery door open at night helps moisture escape and also stops the battery from draining.
For rechargeable aids, the drying and charging method recommended by the manufacturer is followed.
A wax guard is a small filter that sits in the sound outlet of the receiver and stops earwax from getting into the receiver.
It is changed with a small tool from the manufacturer that has one empty end and a new filter on the other end.
First the dome or earmold is removed from the receiver tip, leaving the filter exposed.
The empty end of the tool is pressed into the old filter and pulled straight out.
The new filter on the other end of the tool is placed in the receiver outlet, and the tool is gently withdrawn.
The dome is refitted, and the sound of the aid is confirmed with a quick listening check.
How often the filter is changed depends on how much earwax the person makes; it is changed at once when it is blocked.
The fault complaints users bring usually fall into four groups.
The first is a dead aid; the user says no sound comes from the aid at all.
The second is weak sound; the aid works, but the sound is not as strong or clear as before.
The third is crackling, cutting out or distorted sound; the sound comes and goes, or sounds metallic and harsh.
The fourth is whistling; this is a high-pitched sound caused by acoustic feedback.
With a dead aid, the check always starts with the simplest step: the power source.
In a battery aid, a new battery is inserted or the old one is tested; a rechargeable aid is confirmed to be really charged.
Next, check whether the aid is switched on, the volume level, and whether it has slipped into a silent program by mistake.
Then the sound outlet is examined; the wax guard, dome or earmold may be blocked with earwax.
In a behind-the-ear aid, the tubing is also checked for water droplets, kinks or cracks.
Finally, check whether the microphone inlet is blocked by dust or dirt.
If the aid is still dead after these steps, the internal parts need a service assessment.
The most common cause of weak sound is a wax guard partly blocked with earwax; once it is changed, the sound often returns.
A microphone inlet blocked with dust or dirt also weakens the sound, and it especially hurts understanding in noise.
With crackling and cutting out, a weak battery and moisture come first; the battery is replaced and the aid is dried.
In a receiver-in-canal aid, if the sound cuts out when the receiver wire is moved, the wire or its connection may be damaged.
With whistling, first check whether the dome or earmold sits properly in the ear; a loose fit lets sound leak out.
Earwax blocking the ear canal, or impacted cerumen, can also reflect sound back and cause whistling, so otoscopy is never skipped.
This table is a starting point; if the complaint continues, the aid is checked electroacoustically in the test box.
Whistling occurs when sound from the receiver leaks out and reaches the microphone again; we saw this earlier in the lesson on feedback.
Impacted earwax in the ear canal reflects sound back instead of passing it to the eardrum, and it can make whistling worse.
In a behind-the-ear aid, tubing that hardens, cracks or comes loose from the earmold over time also lets sound leak.
Talking or chewing can move the earmold slightly, so the whistling may be heard only at those moments.
In children the earmold becomes too small as the ear canal grows; repeated whistling often means a new earmold is needed.
Whistling while the aid is held in the hand or being put in, however, is usually normal and is not a fault.

maddeler.metin: BTE: on the hook or _tubing end_

cumleler: A listening stethoscope is a simple tool that lets the clinician hear the hearing aid's sound with their own ear.
It consists of a binaural tube and a small tip that connects to the aid; it is inexpensive but tells you a great deal.
On a behind-the-ear aid, the tip attaches to the earhook or to the end of the earmold tubing.
For receiver-in-canal and in-the-ear aids, a special adapter that grips the sound outlet is used.
Listening is done in a quiet room, and the aid is turned on at a low volume first to protect the clinician's ear.
Listen for whether the sound is clear, crackly, cutting in and out, or metallic and distorted.
Also listen for dropouts while the aid is gently moved and while the battery compartment or the wire is touched.
Infants and young children who wear aids cannot say the aid is broken, so the daily check is the job of the family and teacher.
First, the aid, earmold and tubing are inspected for wax, moisture and cracks.
Then the parent listens with the stethoscope to make sure the aid's sound is clear and uninterrupted.
Next, the Ling sounds are spoken and heard clearly through the stethoscope; as the child grows, the child's responses are also observed.
Any problem noticed is written down, so a recurring fault is easy to spot.
Any problem that cannot be solved is reported to the clinic the same day; every day without the aid matters for language development.
Care and simple checks are not always enough; in some cases a referral is needed.
If there is no sound or the sound is distorted even after the battery, filter, dome and tubing are checked, the aid is sent for service.
If there is ear pain, discharge, itching, redness or a sore caused by the earmold, the person is referred to a physician.
Earwax blocking the ear canal is also assessed by a physician; the canal must be clear for the aid to work properly.
In doubtful cases, the gain and distortion of the aid are compared objectively in the test box we saw earlier.

sahneler.metin: For any reported fault, check the battery, filter and ear canal first; make sure the aid really works before touching the settings.
cumleler: A tip from the field: with a complaint of weak sound, do not rush to raise the gain or refit the aid.
First check the battery, the wax guard, the dome or tubing, and the ear canal with otoscopy.
If gain is raised instead of changing a blocked filter, the aid will be too loud once the filter is changed, and new complaints begin.
Teach care by practicing it together with the user when the aid is delivered, and give a short written care checklist.
The aid is wiped with a dry cloth every day, the microphone inlet is brushed, and wax is removed from the dome or earmold.
Moisture is the most common hidden cause of faults; drying and proper storage extend the life of the aid.
With a dead aid or weak sound, the check goes in order: battery, settings, wax guard, tubing and microphone.
A listening stethoscope lets the clinician and the family check the aid's sound with their own ears.

sahneler.soru: First check for sudden weak sound in a RIC aid?
sahneler.aciklama: The most common cause of weak sound is a wax guard _blocked with earwax_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: the sound of a receiver-in-canal aid has suddenly become weak. What is checked first?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: the wax guard.
Because the receiver sits in the ear canal, the filter is easily blocked with earwax; once it is changed, the sound often returns.
